newsitem.title: UK: UK to shed up to 2,000 petrol sites in '96 - analyst.
newsitem.headline: UK to shed up to 2,000 petrol sites in '96 - analyst.

text.p: The ferocious retail price war in the British gasoline market will force 1,500 to 2,000 site closures in 1996 and boost market share for the supermarket groups and top four oil company players over the next three years, an oil consultant said.
That compares with an average closure rate of 750 a year over the last four years, according to a recent report by Wood Mackenzie.
Market share for the oil companies and supermarket groups could jump to 85 percent by the year 2000, from 66 percent in 1995, it said.
"One of the most significant outcomes of the war has been the change in dynamics of price setting in the U.K.," said Stephen Brooks, principal consultant and author of the report.

"Price Watch has forced Esso into the role of price follower rather than leader, relinquishing the job of leading up prices to Shell, with the grocers taking the initiative in leading them down from time to time as they skirmish amongst themselves," he said.

Grocers have always been able to exploit their lower cost base to charge lower prices, he said, and "in the future they will have greater influence on overall price setting and therefore margins in the U.K."
Gross margins will also never return to the levels seen before Esso's Price Watch campaign launched a year ago, and marginw will settle in the 3-5 pence per liter range, he said.
The 2-3 pence per litre range reached this summer proved "insufficient to achieve break even for the lowest cost operator and were inevitably unsustainable," he said.
"We believe that as long as the grocers are able to sustain their own volumes, in the medium term they will rely on the use of card loyalty schemes to differentiate themselves..." he said.
He suggested it may be more difficult for oil companies to become a successful retailer than for a professional retailing group to add motor fuels to products it offers.
Oil companies could retrench "back into their traditional role of wholesalers, leaving the larger retail groups to take full control of the forecourts," he said.
